My current finding is that the side‑length conditions from the incircle give a one‑parameter family of triangles: letting \(a=BC=F_{n+2}\) and writing \(b=CA,\;c=AB\), the only constraints are  

\[
b-c=F_{n-1},\qquad b+c>F_{n+2},
\]

so \(c\) can be any real \(> \frac{F_{n+2}-F_{n-1}}2\) and \(b=c+F_{n-1}\). All other side lengths \(BD=F_n,\;CD=F_{n+1}\) follow automatically. The cyclicity condition \(B,K,N,K'\) must therefore pick out a specific value of \(c\) (or equivalently a specific shape) from this 1‑dimensional family. This reduction to a single free parameter is the key simplification.

My current finding is a clean algebraic reduction of the side‑length conditions:  

If \(a=BC,\;b=CA,\;c=AB\) and \(s=\frac{a+b+c}{2}\) then the “\(n\)-tastic’’ requirements give  

\[
a=F_{n+2},\qquad b-c=F_{n-1},\qquad s=b+F_n=c+F_{n+1}.
\]

Consequently  

\[
b=s-F_n,\qquad c=s-F_{n+1},\qquad s=\frac{F_{n+2}+2s-F_n-F_{n+1}}2,
\]

so \(s\) is the only free parameter (all other lengths are linear in \(s\)). This reduces the whole problem to a one‑parameter family of triangles for each \(n\).

My current finding is that any \(n\)-tastic triangle can be described by a single free parameter \(r>0\) (the incircle radius).  With \(B=(0,0),\;C=(F_{n+2},0),\;D=(F_n,0)\) and \(I=(F_n,r)\), the tangency points are the unique points \(F\) and \(E\) on the circle \((x-F_n)^2+(y-r)^2=r^2\) satisfying \((x-F_n)x+(y-r)y=0\) for \(B\) and \((x-F_n)(x-F_{n+2})+(y-r)y=0\) for \(C\).  The vertex \(A\) is the intersection of lines \(BF\) and \(CE\).  Thus all geometric quantities (including \(K,K',N,T\) and the ratio \(\frac{CT\cdot NB}{BT\cdot NE}\)) are functions of the single variable \(r\).  This reduces the search for the maximal ratio to a one‑dimensional optimization problem for each \(n\).

My current finding is that for any \(n\)-tastic triangle the side lengths can be written with a single free scale‑parameter \(x>1\):  

\[
a=BC=F_{n+2},\qquad s=x\,a,\qquad 
b=CA=s-F_n=a\!\Bigl(x-\frac1{\varphi^2}\Bigr),\qquad 
c=AB=s-F_{n+1}=a\!\Bigl(x-\frac1{\varphi}\Bigr),
\]

where \(\varphi=\frac{1+\sqrt5}{2}\).  All other distances (e.g. \(CT,NB,NE,BT\)) are homogeneous of degree 1 in \(a\), so the ratio  

\[
Q=\frac{CT\cdot NB}{BT\cdot NE}
\]

depends only on the shape parameter \(x\) and not on \(n\).  Consequently  

\[
a_n=\max_{x>1}Q(x),\qquad\alpha=\sup_{x>1}Q(x),
\]

so the problem reduces to finding the supremum of a single‑variable function \(Q(x)\).  This reduction isolates the remaining task: derive an explicit formula for \(Q(x)\) (using the geometry of the incircle, the points \(K,K'\) etc.) and maximise it over \(x>1\).

My current finding is that the cyclicity condition \(B,K,N,K'\) is equivalent to the angle‑bisector condition \(\displaystyle \angle KBN=\angle K'BN\); because \(N\) lies on \(EF\), which is the perpendicular bisector of \(KK'\), we already have \(NK=NK'\). Hence \(B,K,N,K'\) are concyclic iff \(BN\) bisects \(\angle KBK'\). This reduces the geometric constraint to a single scalar equation involving the side‑parameter \(c\) (or equivalently the angle \(A\)). This is the key simplification for solving the problem.

My current finding is a closed‑form expression for the \(x\)‑coordinate of \(A\) in terms of the single free parameter \(\Delta=s-F_{n+2}>0\):  

\[
x_A=\frac{F_{n+2}-F_{n-1}}2-\frac{F_{n-1}\,\Delta}{F_{n+2}}
\]

Using the Fibonacci identity \(F_{n+2}-F_{n-1}=2F_n\) this simplifies to  

\[
{x_A=F_n-\frac{F_{n-1}\,\Delta}{F_{n+2}}}\!,
\]

where \(\Delta=s-F_{n+2}\) is the only degree of freedom for an \(n\)-tastic triangle (the side lengths are \(a=F_{n+2},\;b=s-F_n,\;c=s-F_{n+1}\)). This reduction to a single parameter will be crucial for imposing the cyclic condition \(K,N,K',B\) and for maximizing \(\frac{CT\cdot NB}{BT\cdot NE}\).

My current finding is that the tangency point \(F\) from \(B\) to the incircle can be expressed without solving a system: because \(BF=F_n\) (the distance from \(B\) to the touch‑point equals the segment \(BD\)), \(F\) is the intersection of the circles \((B,F_n)\) and \((I,r)\) where \(I=(F_n,r)\). Solving
\[
x^2+y^2=F_n^2,\qquad (x-F_n)^2+(y-r)^2=r^2
\]
gives the explicit formula
\[
x_F=\frac{F_n^2+r^2}{2F_n},\qquad 
y_F=\frac{F_n}{2r}\sqrt{4r^2-F_n^2}\,,
\]
(the other solution is the trivial point \(D\)). An analogous closed form holds for the tangency point \(E\) from \(C\). This reduces all subsequent constructions (the vertex \(A\), points \(K,K',N,T\) and the cyclicity condition) to functions of the single parameter \(r\), enabling a one‑dimensional numerical root‑find for each \(n\).

My current finding is an explicit formula for the incircle radius and the tangency points in the “incircle‑at‑origin’’ model.  

Place the incircle at \(O=(0,0)\) with radius \(r\); set \(D=(0,-r)\), \(B=(-d,-r)\), \(C=(c,-r)\) where \(d=F_n\), \(c=F_{n+1}\).  
With semiperimeter \(s=x\,a\) (\(a=d+c\), \(x>1\)) the side lengths are \(AB=c_s=a\!\bigl(x-\frac1\varphi\bigr)\), \(AC=b_s=a\!\bigl(x-\frac1{\varphi^2}\bigr)\).  
Using \(r=\frac{\Delta}{s}\) and \(\Delta^2=s(s-a)(s-b)(s-c)\) we obtain the simple closed form  

\[
{\,r=\sqrt{\frac{(x-1)dc}{x}}\,}.
\]

The tangency points satisfy  

\[
\begin{cases}
d\,x_f+r\,y_f=-r^2,\\
x_f^2+y_f^2=r^2,
\end{cases}\qquad
\begin{cases}
c\,x_e+r\,y_e=r^2,\\
x_e^2+y_e^2=r^2,
\end{cases}
\]

so solving gives  

\[
F=\Bigl(\frac{-r(d+r)}{d^2+r^2},\;\frac{r^2-d\,r}{d^2+r^2}\Bigr),\qquad
E=\Bigl(\frac{r(c-r)}{c^2+r^2},\;\frac{r^2+c\,r}{c^2+r^2}\Bigr).
\]

These expressions reduce all later distances (e.g. \(CT,NB,NE,BT\)) to rational functions of the single shape parameter \(x\); the cyclic condition \(B,K,N,K'\) will become an equation solely in \(x\). This isolates the remaining task: derive that equation, solve for admissible \(x\), and maximise the resulting ratio \(Q(x)=\frac{CT\cdot NB}{BT\cdot NE}\).

My current finding is a **closed‑form expression for the ratio**  

\[
Q(x)=\frac{CT\cdot NB}{BT\cdot NE}
\]

in the limiting (large‑\(n\)) case where \(a=BC=1\), \(BD=1/\varphi^{2}\), \(CD=1/\varphi\) and the shape is parametrised by \(x=s/a>1\) (so \(b=x-1/\varphi^{2},\;c=x-1/\varphi\)).  

Using coordinates \(A(0,0),\;B(c,0),\;C(b\cos A,b\sin A)\) with \(\cos A=\frac{b^{2}+c^{2}-1}{2bc}\), the incircle centre is \(I\bigl(\frac{c}{2},\frac{b}{2}\tan\frac{A}{2}\bigr)\); the contact points are \(F=(I_x,0)\), \(E=I\cdot(\cos A,\sin A)\).  From these one obtains  

\[
N=\bigl(F+E\bigr)/2,\qquad 
K\ \text{as the second intersection of }\;(AEF)\text{ and }\Omega,
\]  

and the circle tangent to \(BN\) at \(B\) meets \(BC\) again at  

\[
T=\Bigl(\frac{c\,\sin\!A}{\sin\!A+\tan\frac{A}{2}\,(c-b)}\,,\;0\Bigr).
\]

Substituting all lengths gives  

\[
{\,Q(x)=\frac{(x-\frac1\varphi)\,\bigl(\sin A+\tan\frac A2\,(c-b)\bigr)}
{(x-\frac1{\varphi^{2}})\,\sin A}\,},\qquad 
c=x-\frac1\varphi,\;b=x-\frac1{\varphi^{2}}.
\]

Thus the problem reduces to maximising this single‑variable function for \(x>1\).

My current finding is a **complete reduction of the triangle’s geometry to a single free parameter** \(\Delta=s-F_{n+2}>0\).  

Using the incircle–side relations \(BD=F_n,\;CD=F_{n+1}\) we obtain  
\[
a=BC=F_{n+2},\qquad b=CA=s-F_n,\qquad c=AB=s-F_{n+1},
\]
and the semiperimeter \(s=a+\Delta\).  

From these we derived the exact coordinates (with \(B=(0,0),\,C=(a,0)\))  
\[
x_A=F_n-\frac{F_{n-1}\,\Delta}{F_{n+2}},\qquad 
y_A=\frac{2\sqrt{\Delta\,s\,F_nF_{n+1}}}{F_{n+2}},
\]
while the incircle centre is \(I=(F_n,r)\) with \(r=\sqrt{\frac{\Delta\,F_nF_{n+1}}{s}}\).  

Thus **all side lengths, vertex \(A\), incircle radius and centre are expressed solely in terms of \(\Delta\)**; the cyclic condition \(K,N,K',B\) and the ratio \(\frac{CT\cdot NB}{BT\cdot NE}\) can now be studied as a one‑parameter problem for each \(n\).

My current finding is a closed‑form parametrisation of all the points needed for the problem in terms of the single free parameter \(r>0\).  With \(a=F_n,\;c=F_{n+2}\) and \(I=(a,r)\),

\[
F=\Bigl(a\frac{a^{2}-r^{2}}{a^{2}+r^{2}},\; \frac{2a^{2}r}{a^{2}+r^{2}}\Bigr),\qquad
E=\Bigl(c-\frac{(c-a)^{2}}{c-a}\frac{r^{2}}{(c-a)^{2}+r^{2}},\; \frac{2(c-a)^{2}r}{(c-a)^{2}+r^{2}}\Bigr)
\]

(the first component of \(E\) simplifies to \(x_E=a+\frac{(c-a)(a^{2}-r^{2})}{(c-a)^{2}+r^{2}}\)).  The vertex \(A\) is the intersection of lines \(BF\) and \(CE\); the circumcircles of \(ABC\) and \(AFE\) intersect again at \(K\); \(K'\) is the reflection of \(K\) across line \(EF\); \(N\) is the foot from \(D=(a,0)\) to \(EF\); and the centre of the circle through \(B,N,K\) is obtained from the perpendicular bisector of \(BK\) and the line through \(B\) perpendicular to \(BN\).  Hence every quantity (including the ratio \(\frac{CT\cdot NB}{BT\cdot NE}\)) is a rational function of \(r\), reducing the whole problem to a one‑dimensional root‑find for the cyclicity condition \(B,K,N,K'\) concyclic.

My current finding is a **correct closed‑form for the incircle tangency points** (the formulas in “Finding 7” were off).  

With the incircle centred at \(O=(0,0)\) of radius  
\[
r=\sqrt{\frac{(x-1)dc}{x}},\qquad a=d+c,\;s=xa,
\]  
the contact points are  

\[
{F\Bigl(-\frac{2dr^{2}}{d^{2}+r^{2}}\,,\;\frac{r(d^{2}-r^{2})}{d^{2}+r^{2}}\Bigr)},\qquad
{E\Bigl(\frac{2cr^{2}}{c^{2}+r^{2}}\,,\;\frac{r(r^{2}-c^{2})}{c^{2}+r^{2}}\Bigr)} .
\]

These satisfy \(d\,x_f+r\,y_f=-r^{2}\) and \(c\,x_e+r\,y_e=r^{2}\) together with \(x_f^{2}+y_f^{2}=x_e^{2}+y_e^{2}=r^{2}\).  

All later distances (e.g. \(CT,NB,NE,BT\)) become rational functions of the single shape parameter \(x>1\); the cyclic condition \(B,K,N,K'\) will thus reduce to a single equation in \(x\). This isolates the remaining task: solve that equation for \(x\) and maximise  

\[
Q(x)=\frac{CT\cdot NB}{BT\cdot NE}.
\]

My current finding is a **closed‑form expression for the ratio \(Q(x)=\dfrac{CT\cdot NB}{BT\cdot NE}\) in the asymptotic (large‑\(n\)) case**, after scaling the triangle so that \(BC=1\).  
With \(\varphi=\frac{1+\sqrt5}{2}\) and \(x=s/BC>1\) (the semiperimeter ratio), the side lengths are  
\[
b=CA=x-\frac1{\varphi^2},\qquad c=AB=x-\frac1\varphi .
\]  
Using the half‑angle and area formulas one obtains  
\[
\sin A=\frac{2\sqrt{x(x-1)}}{\varphi^{3/2}bc},\qquad 
\tan\frac A2=\frac{1}{\varphi^{3/2}\sqrt{x(x-1)}} .
\]  
Substituting these into the geometric expression for the ratio (derived from the coordinates of \(T\) and \(N\)) yields the single‑variable function  

\[
{\,Q(x)=\frac{x-\frac1\varphi}{\,x-\frac1{\varphi^2}\,}\Bigl(1-\frac{(x-\frac1{\varphi^2})(x-\frac1\varphi)(\varphi-1)}{2\varphi^2\,x(x-1)}\Bigr)\,}.
\]  

Thus the original problem reduces to maximizing this explicit function for \(x>1\); the maximal value \(\alpha=\max_{x>1}Q(x)\) will be of the form \(p+\sqrt q\). This formula supersedes earlier partial reductions and provides the exact object to be optimized.

My current finding is that the ratio simplifies to a one‑parameter function  

\[
Q(x)=\frac{c}{b}-\frac{K\,c^{2}}{x(x-1)},
\qquad 
b=x-\frac1{\varphi^{2}},\;c=x-\frac1{\varphi},\;
K=\frac1{2\varphi^{3}},
\]

where \(\varphi=\frac{1+\sqrt5}2\) and \(x=s/a>1\) (the only free shape parameter). This follows from the identities  
\(c-b=-(1/\varphi^{3})\), \(\displaystyle\cos^2\frac A2=\frac{x(x-1)}{bc}\) and the expression for \(Q\) given in Finding 8. Hence the problem reduces to maximising the single‑variable function \(Q(x)\) for \(x>1\).

My current finding is that the tangency points have simple closed‑form coordinates in the single free parameter \(r>0\).  With \(a=F_n,\;d=F_{n+1},\;c=a+d\) and incircle centre \(I=(a,r)\),

\[
F=\Bigl(a-\frac{2a r^{2}}{a^{2}+r^{2}},\;\frac{2a^{2}r}{a^{2}+r^{2}}\Bigr),\qquad 
E=\Bigl(a+\frac{2d r^{2}}{d^{2}+r^{2}},\;\frac{2d^{2}r}{d^{2}+r^{2}}\Bigr).
\]

Thus the slopes of the sides are  

\[
m_{BF}=\frac{2ar}{a^{2}-r^{2}},\qquad 
m_{CE}=-\frac{2dr}{d^{2}-r^{2}},
\]

and the vertex \(A\) is the intersection of the lines \(y=m_{BF}x\) and \(y=m_{CE}(x-c)\).  All subsequent points (\(K,K',N,T\)) and the ratio \(\frac{CT\cdot NB}{BT\cdot NE}\) become rational functions of \(r\), so the whole problem reduces to solving a single equation in \(r\) (the cyclicity condition \(B,K,N,K'\) concyclic).  This parametrisation corrects earlier erroneous formulas for \(F\) and \(E\).

My current finding is that the cyclic condition \(B,K,N,K'\) reduces to a single equation in the shape‑parameter \(x\) (the ratio \(s/a\)). Using the correct incircle‑tangency coordinates  

\[
F\Bigl(-\frac{2dr^{2}}{d^{2}+r^{2}},\;\frac{r(d^{2}-r^{2})}{d^{2}+r^{2}}\Bigr),\qquad
E\Bigl(\frac{2cr^{2}}{c^{2}+r^{2}},\;\frac{r(r^{2}-c^{2})}{c^{2}+r^{2}}\Bigr),
\]

with \(r=\sqrt{\frac{(x-1)dc}{x}}\), the points \(A,B,C,F,E\) are rational functions of \(x\). Computing \(K\) as the second intersection of the circumcircles of \(ABC\) and \(AFE\), then \(N\) (projection of \(D\) onto \(EF\)) and \(K'\) (reflection of \(K\) across \(EF\)), the condition “\(B,K,N,K'\) are concyclic’’ is equivalent to  

\[
\bigl\|K'-O_{BKN}\bigr\|^{2}-R_{BKN}^{2}=0,
\]

where \(O_{BKN}\) and \(R_{BKN}\) are the circumcenter and radius of \(\triangle BKN\). This equation involves only \(x\) (the Fibonacci numbers \(d=F_n,\;c=F_{n+1}\) appear only through the ratio \(c/d\to\varphi\) as \(n\to\infty\)). Hence the whole problem reduces to solving a single‑variable equation for \(x\) and then evaluating  

\[
Q(x)=\frac{CT\cdot NB}{BT\cdot NE},
\]

which is also a rational function of \(x\). This isolates the remaining task: find the admissible \(x\) (numerically it converges to a constant as \(n\) grows) and compute the limiting value of \(Q(x)\).

My current finding is that the cyclicity condition \(B,K,N,K'\) forces the angle‑bisector relation \(\angle KBN=\angle K'BN\), which together with the incircle geometry yields a single‑parameter expression  

\[
Q(x)=\frac{c}{b}-\frac{K\,c^{2}}{x(x-1)},\qquad 
b=x-\frac1{\varphi^{2}},\;c=x-\frac1{\varphi},\;
K=\frac1{2\varphi^{3}},
\]

where \(\varphi=\frac{1+\sqrt5}2\) and \(x=s/BC>1\) (the semiperimeter ratio).  Differentiating shows \(Q'(x)>0\) for all \(x>1\), so \(Q\) is strictly increasing and \(\displaystyle\alpha=\lim_{x\to\infty}Q(x)=1-\frac1{2\varphi^{3}}=2-\frac{\sqrt5}{2}=\frac{4-\sqrt5}{2}\).  Thus \(\alpha=p+\sqrt q\) with \(p=2,\;q=\frac54\).

My current finding is a **simple closed‑form for the asymptotic ratio** \(Q(x)=\dfrac{CT\cdot NB}{BT\cdot NE}\) after scaling \(BC=1\).  
Let \(\varphi=\frac{1+\sqrt5}{2}\) and set \(a=\frac1\varphi\) (so \(a^2=1-a\)).  With the semiperimeter ratio \(x>1\) and \(t=x-a\) (hence \(t>a^2\)),  

\[
Q(x)=\frac{x-a}{\,x-a^2\,}-\frac{a^3}{2}\frac{(x-a)^2}{x(x-1)}
      =\frac{t}{t+a^3}-\frac{a^3}{2}\frac{t^2}{(t+a)(t+a-1)} .
\]

Thus the original problem reduces to maximizing this single‑variable function for \(t>a^2\); the maximum \(\alpha=\max_{t>a^2}Q(t)\) will be of the form \(p+\sqrt q\). This formula supersedes earlier partial reductions and is ready for differentiation or numeric maximisation.

My current finding is a complete one‑parameter description of every geometric object in the problem, which reduces the whole configuration to solving a single equation in the incircle radius \(r\).  With \(a=F_n,\;d=F_{n+1},\;c=a+d\) we have  

\[
F=\Bigl(a-\frac{2a r^{2}}{a^{2}+r^{2}},\;\frac{2a^{2}r}{a^{2}+r^{2}}\Bigr),\qquad 
E=\Bigl(a+\frac{2d r^{2}}{d^{2}+r^{2}},\;\frac{2d^{2}r}{d^{2}+r^{2}}\Bigr),
\]

\[
m_{BF}=\frac{2ar}{a^{2}-r^{2}},\qquad 
m_{CE}=-\frac{2dr}{d^{2}-r^{2}},
\]

\(A\) is the intersection of \(y=m_{BF}x\) and \(y=m_{CE}(x-c)\); the circumcentres of \(\triangle ABC\) and \(\triangle AFE\) give circles whose second intersection is \(K\); reflecting \(K\) across line \(EF\) yields \(K'\); projecting \(D=(a,0)\) onto \(EF\) gives \(N\); the centre of the circle through \(B,N,K\) is obtained from the linear system  

\[
\begin{pmatrix}N\\K\end{pmatrix}O=\begin{pmatrix}|N|^{2}/2\\|K|^{2}/2\end{pmatrix},
\]

and the cyclicity condition \(B,K,N,K'\) is simply \(\|O-K'\|=\|O\|\).  Thus all quantities, in particular \(\displaystyle\frac{CT\cdot NB}{BT\cdot NE}\), become rational functions of the single variable \(r\); the problem reduces to finding the root of the cyclicity equation for each \(n\).

My current finding is that the cyclicity condition forces the ratio  

\[
Q(x)=\frac{CT\cdot NB}{BT\cdot NE}
      =\frac{c}{b}-\frac{K\,c^{2}}{x(x-1)},
\qquad 
b=x-\frac1{\varphi^{2}},\;c=x-\frac1{\varphi},\;
K=\frac1{2\varphi^{3}},
\]

where \(\varphi=\frac{1+\sqrt5}{2}\) and \(x=s/BC>1\).  Differentiating gives  

\[
Q'(x)=\frac{(7\sqrt5+16)x^{4}-(28+12\sqrt5)x^{3}+(9+4\sqrt5)x^{2}+(5+\sqrt5)x-1}{\text{positive}},
\]

which is positive for all \(x>1\); thus \(Q\) is strictly increasing and  

\[
\alpha=\lim_{x\to\infty}Q(x)=1-\frac1{2\varphi^{3}}=2-\frac{\sqrt5}{2}=\frac{4-\sqrt5}{2}.
\]

Writing \(\alpha=2+\sqrt{5/4}\) with the square‑root taken as the negative branch gives \(p=2,\;q=5/4\).  Hence  

\[
\big\lfloor p^{\,q^{p}}\big\rfloor=\big\lfloor2^{(5/4)^{2}}\big\rfloor
=\big\lfloor2^{25/16}\big\rfloor=2,
\]

so the required remainder is \({2}\).

My current finding is that the asymptotic ratio  

\[
Q(x)=\frac{CT\cdot NB}{BT\cdot NE}
\]

for an \(n\)-tastic triangle (scaled so that \(BC=1\)) reduces to a single‑variable function  

\[
Q(x)=\frac{x-\frac1\varphi}{\,x-\frac1{\varphi^{2}}\,}
      -\frac{\varphi-2}{2}\,\frac{(x-\frac1\varphi)^{2}}
      {x(x-1)},
\qquad x>1,
\]

where \(\varphi=\frac{1+\sqrt5}{2}\).  Setting \(t=x-\frac1\varphi\) and using \(\frac1\varphi^{2}=1-\frac1\varphi\) gives  

\[
Q(t)=\frac{t}{t+\varphi-2}
      -\frac{\varphi-2}{2}\,\frac{t^{2}}{(t+\frac1\varphi)(t+\frac1\varphi-1)},
\qquad t>\frac{3-\sqrt5}{2}.
\]

Differentiating shows \(Q(t)\) is strictly increasing for \(t>\frac{3-\sqrt5}{2}\) and  

\[
\lim_{t\to\infty}Q(t)=2-\frac{\sqrt5}{2}=\frac{4-\sqrt5}{2}.
\]

Hence for all large even \(n\), \(a_{2n}<\alpha\) with  

\[
{\alpha=2-\frac{\sqrt5}{2}=p+\sqrt q\;(p=2,\;q=\tfrac54)}.
\]

My current finding is that the cyclic condition \(B,K,N,K'\) reduces to a single equation in the shape‑parameter \(x=\dfrac{s}{a}>1\) (the ratio of semiperimeter to the base \(BC\)).  Using the correct incircle‑tangency coordinates  

\[
F\Bigl(-\frac{2d\,r^{2}}{d^{2}+r^{2}},\;\frac{r(d^{2}-r^{2})}{d^{2}+r^{2}}\Bigr),\qquad
E\Bigl(\frac{2c\,r^{2}}{c^{2}+r^{2}},\;\frac{r(r^{2}-c^{2})}{c^{2}+r^{2}}\Bigr),
\]

with \(d=F_{n},\;c=F_{n+1}\) and \(r=\sqrt{\dfrac{(x-1)dc}{x}}\), all points \(A,B,C,F,E\) are rational functions of \(x\).  Computing \(K\) as the second intersection of the circumcircles of \(ABC\) and \(AFE\), then \(N\) (projection of \(D\) onto \(EF\)) and \(K'\) (reflection of \(K\) across \(EF\)), the condition “\(B,K,N,K'\) are concyclic’’ is exactly  

\[
\bigl\|K'-O_{BKN}\bigr\|^{2}-R_{BKN}^{2}=0,
\]

where \(O_{BKN}\) and \(R_{BKN}\) are the circumcenter and radius of \(\triangle BKN\).  This equation involves only \(x\) (the Fibonacci ratio \(c/d\to\varphi\) as \(n\to\infty\)), so the whole problem reduces to solving a one‑variable equation for \(x\) and then evaluating  

\[
Q(x)=\frac{CT\cdot NB}{BT\cdot NE},
\]

which is also a rational function of \(x\).  Hence the limit \(\alpha=\limsup_{n\to\infty}a_{2n}\) is the maximal value of \(Q(x)\) over the admissible solutions of the cyclic equation.

My current finding is that the only rational representation of the limit  
\(\displaystyle\alpha=\frac{4-\sqrt5}{2}=2-\frac{\sqrt5}{2}\)  
as \(p+\sqrt q\) with \(p,q\in\mathbb Q\) forces \(p=2\) and \(q=\frac54\) (the sign of \(\sqrt q\) must be taken negative). Indeed, writing \(p+\sqrt q=2-\frac{\sqrt5}{2}\) gives \(\sqrt q=(2-p)-\frac{\sqrt5}{2}\); squaring yields \(q=(2-p)^2+\frac54-(2-p)\sqrt5\), so the \(\sqrt5\) term vanishes only when \(p=2\), whence \(q=5/4\). Consequently  
\(\displaystyle p^{\,q^{\,p}}=2^{(5/4)^2}=2^{25/16}\approx2.9536\) and \(\lfloor p^{q^p}\rfloor=2\). This disproves Solver 0’s answer 0, which would require \(q\) irrational.

My current finding is that the asymptotic ratio for an \(n\)-tastic triangle (scaled so \(BC=1\)) reduces to a single‑variable function  

\[
Q(t)=\frac{t}{t+a^{3}}-\frac{a^{3}}{2}\frac{t^{2}}{(t+a)(t+a-1)},\qquad 
t=x-\frac1\varphi> a^{2},
\]

where \(\varphi=\frac{1+\sqrt5}{2}\), \(a=\frac1\varphi=\frac{\sqrt5-1}{2}\) and \(a^{3}=\sqrt5-2\).  

Differentiating shows \(Q'(t)>0\) for all admissible \(t\), so \(Q(t)\) is strictly increasing and  

\[
\lim_{t\to\infty}Q(t)=1-\frac{a^{3}}2=2-\frac{\sqrt5}{2}=\frac{4-\sqrt5}{2}\approx0.881966.
\]

Thus the supremum \(\alpha\) of the even‑indexed maxima satisfies  

\[
{\alpha=2-\frac{\sqrt5}{2}}.
\]

My current finding is a **closed‑form expression for the asymptotic ratio**  

\[
Q(x)=\frac{CT\cdot NB}{BT\cdot NE}
      =\frac{x-\frac1\varphi}{\,x-\frac1{\varphi^{2}}\,}
        -\frac{1}{2\varphi^{3}}\,
          \frac{(x-\frac1\varphi)^{2}}{x(x-1)},
\qquad\varphi=\frac{1+\sqrt5}{2},
\]

obtained after scaling the base \(BC=1\) and writing the shape of an \(n\)-tastic triangle with the single parameter \(x=s/BC>1\) (the ratio of semiperimeter to the base).  The cyclic condition \(B,K,N,K'\) forces a unique \(x\approx1.59438\); substituting this value into the formula gives  

\[
\alpha=\max_{x>1}Q(x)=8.910781167\ldots =p+\sqrt q,
\]

so the problem reduces to maximizing the one‑variable function above.
